title: Natural Hypertrophy: my lifting philosophy
summary: NH explains that he cares about size, not the weight on the bar or the specific lift, yet as a natural you must get stronger to get bigger. He uses squat, bench and deadlift with all their variations plus accessories as a base, only chases strength when size stalls, and treats strict form as non-negotiable, citing his own partial-lockout choices on squat and overhead press.

claims.claim: NH doesn't care about the weight on the bar or which lift he does; given the choice between a 500 lb bench and a big chest he would pick the big chest.
As a natural lifter, bodybuilder or not, the only way to get bigger is to get stronger: not necessarily a 600 lb deadlift, but you must progress on certain lifts to add size.
Squat, bench and deadlift are not necessarily the best lifts, but used smartly they are a solid base for any bodybuilding program and most bodybuilders should do them.
Take each main lift and use its variations: for the squat, back squat plus paused back squat, front squat and other variants, rotating them to reach your goals.
Doing only squat, bench and deadlift (popularised by powerlifting) can get you big, as it did for NH, but it will get you injured; you also need accessories, variations and unrelated lifts.
Some of NH's lifts are terrible relative to his size, e.g. overhead pressing one plate (135 lb) at about 200 lb bodyweight, yet he has big shoulders so it doesn't bother him.
He only puts effort into gaining strength on a lift when size stops catching up; as long as the muscle grows he leaves the load alone.
He has squatted 365 lb for a long time while his legs keep growing, so he changes nothing; if they stopped growing he would force more weight to stimulate growth.
Form is the most important thing: better to lift 300 lb with good form than 500 lb with poor form, because form keeps you injury free, in control, and stimulating the target muscle.
If he senses form breaking down, e.g. on a deadlift, he stops and puts the bar down; form breakdown has no upside for bodybuilders.
On the squat he never fully locks out the knees, to keep tension on the legs.
On overhead press he never fully locks the elbows because the bottom of the lift is where the shoulders work most; he presses for shoulder growth, not triceps.
